messages.text: Hey guys, do I need to replace the screen on my bc04 to get harloOS on it?
Used the heliumdeploy-ops-knowledge skill
Read harlolabs.com
Searched the web · Harlo OS Hammer BC04 flash screen replacement required
Searched the web · harlolabs.com BC04 install guide download mode
Read heliumdeploy.com/blogs/mining-news/harlo-os

Hi John,

No, you do not need to buy or replace the screen. Nothing about Harlo OS needs different hardware. The B.04 is on the supported list as it ships, and the only reason the screen comes up in the instructions is that it sits over the USB port on the board.

That is where your flashing trouble probably comes from.
The install steps say to open the flasher in Chrome or Edge, pick your device profile, plug the miner in, take the screen off or connect the USB port directly, then erase and install.
 On the BC04 the display module plugs onto the same header the serial lines use, and while it is seated it can hold those lines and keep the chip from latching into download mode. That matches exactly what you saw: the board enumerates as a USB JTAG serial device, but neither button puts it into boot mode.

So the order I would try next is this. Power the miner down and unplug the yellow XT connector completely. Unclip the screen module from its header and set it aside, nothing is soldered, it comes back on afterwards. Then connect USB only, with no main power, open the flasher, pick the BC04 profile and run the factory image. With the screen off and the board running on USB alone, the firmware is not fighting you for the reset line, and that is usually the point where the port finally shows up as a plain ESP32 in download mode.

Worth saying plainly so you do not waste another evening on it: the OTA route is a dead end on your unit. That 0xE9 rejection means the stock Hammer updater only accepts its own encrypted vendor package, so the plain Harlo image will always be refused there. USB with the screen off is the path.

If it still refuses after that, the fastest help is the Harlo Labs Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf , where JD is @nullhashrate. He wrote the flasher and has seen every stubborn BC04 there is, and people post photos of the header so you can compare against yours.

Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support

Hi John,

That log is more encouraging than it looks. The chip is detected cleanly as an ESP32-S3 with its MAC and crystal read correctly, and the stub uploads and runs. So the cable, the port and the board are all fine. What fails is later in the session: the chip drops out of download mode partway through, starts its normal boot, and esptool reads the boot banner instead of a protocol reply. The 0x45 it complains about is the letter E, the first character of the ROM's own "ESP-ROM:esp32..." startup line. Espressif confirm that reading in their own esptool issue tracker, and their standard suggestion for a stub that connects and then falls over is to skip the stub entirely with the --no-stub option.

That is what I would do next, from the command line rather than the browser flasher, because Web Serial controls the reset lines itself and you cannot override it. On your Mac, install the tool once with pip3 install esptool. Keep the yellow XT power unplugged, screen off, USB only. Hold the boot button down, plug the USB in while still holding it, then release after about two seconds. Then run the flash with the stub disabled and a slow baud rate, something like esptool --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/cu.usbmodem83401 --no-stub --baud 115200 --before no_reset --after no_reset write_flash 0x0 and then the path to the Harlo factory bin you downloaded for the BC04.

The three pieces that matter there are --no-stub, 115200 instead of the default high speed, and --before no_reset, which stops esptool from toggling the reset line and kicking the chip back into normal boot. It is slower, a few minutes rather than one, but it is the combination that gets stubborn S3 boards through. If it still stops at the same point, run the same command with --trace added and send me the last twenty lines or so, because the trace shows exactly which byte it was on when the chip walked away.

I have also passed the whole history on this unit to JD, our hardware lead, who wrote the flasher. He picks it up tomorrow from 10am Eastern and the reply comes to you in this thread. If you want it sorted tonight, he is quickest in the Harlo Labs Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf as @nullhashrate, and the BC04 owners in there have hit this same wall.

Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support

Hi John,

This one is good news, and I want to be precise about why. There is no 0x45 anywhere in that trace. The sync command goes out, the chip answers, esptool reads the eFuse and register blocks and prints the chip ID cleanly, and it keeps answering every single command after that. The chip stayed in download mode for the whole session this time, which is exactly what was failing before. So --no-stub with --before no_reset did the job, and the file name tells me you have the right image, the BC04 factory build.

Your paste stops mid-trace, so one of two things happened: either the mail client clipped it, or it was still running when you copied. Expect it to be slow. Without the stub, at 115200 baud, a factory image of that size writes at roughly 30 to 40 kilobytes per second, so figure somewhere between five and fifteen minutes of actual writing. With --trace switched on, thousands of lines scroll past and the progress percentage is buried in the noise, so it looks frozen when it is working perfectly. Do not touch the board, the cable or the terminal while it does this. Let it run until the prompt comes back.

What finishing looks like is a line reading Wrote so many bytes at 0x00000000, then Hash of data verified, then Leaving. Those three are your confirmation.

If you want a cleaner run, launch it again without --trace and with the last flag changed, so --no-stub --before no_reset --after hard_reset. Dropping the trace gives you a normal progress bar, and hard_reset makes the chip reboot itself at the end instead of sitting there. If you stay on --after no_reset, the unit will just sit quiet when the write finishes, which is not a failure: pull the USB, put the screen back on its header, reconnect the XT power, and it will come up on the new firmware and run its self test on its own.

If it does stop partway with a new error, send me the last twenty lines or so and the byte offset it reached, since a failure at a consistent offset means something quite different from a random one. JD has the full history of this unit as well and is on from 10am Eastern, and he is reachable sooner in the Harlo Labs Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf as @nullhashrate.

Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support

Hi John,

Ha, no, you found the actual answer. That last line is the whole mystery solved, and it is the one result I could not have guessed from the earlier symptoms.

Secure Boot is burned into your unit's ESP32-S3. That is a permanent eFuse setting Hammer applied at the factory, not a setting in the firmware. With it on, the ROM checks a cryptographic signature before it will run the bootloader, and esptool refuses to write anything below 0x8000 because that is where the bootloader lives. It also explains the two dead ends before this. The O. that rejected your file with 0xE9 was demanding Hammer's signed and encrypted container, and the button tricks could never have helped, because the block was never the serial port. The hardware was doing its job the whole time.

Please do not use --force. I want to be blunt about this one. On a part with Secure Boot fused, forcing an unsigned bootloader into place does not give you Harlo OS, it gives you a chip that refuses to run anything at all, including the stock firmware, and there is no way back from it. Download mode will still enumerate and you will still be able to talk to the ROM, but the chip will not boot unsigned code ever again. The warning esptool prints is not boilerplate. Flashing the Harlo app on its own to an OTA offset does not get around it either, since the app has to carry a valid signature too.

So the honest position tonight is that your particular BC04 cannot take Harlo OS by any route I can give you, and the unit you have is perfectly healthy and hashing on its stock firmware. Nothing you did caused this and nothing is broken.

What I do not know is whether there is a signed build for secure-boot BC04 units, or whether this hardware revision is simply off the list. That is JD's call, he builds Harlo OS and deals directly with Hammer, and I have sent him your full trace and that error line. He picks this up from 10am Eastern tomorrow and the answer comes back to you in this thread. If you want it tonight he is in the Harlo Labs Discord as @nullhashrate at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf , and honestly a fused-secure-boot BC04 is the kind of find he will want to see straight away. Worth mentioning your MAC starts e0:72:a1, since the batch may be the distinguishing detail.

Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support

Yes, right here in this thread, no new message or form needed from you. I have put your trace and the Secure Boot error back in front of him with a nudge, since two days without an answer is longer than you should have waited. He is on from 10am Eastern tomorrow and his reply lands in this same thread.

The one question waiting on him is narrow: whether a signed Harlo build exists for BC04 units that left the factory with Secure Boot fused, or whether that revision is simply not flashable. I cannot answer that one honestly, and I would rather you got a real yes or no than a guess from me.

If you would rather not wait, the Harlo Labs Discord is where he is quickest, https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf , as @nullhashrate. Paste the Secure Boot line and your MAC prefix and he will recognise it immediately.

In the meantime your miner is fine as it stands, and nothing you tried has harmed it. Still worth repeating one thing: whatever anyone suggests, do not run that flash with --force.
